key_finding: SciFact establishes scientific claim verification as a task and shows baseline models can identify plausible evidence for 23/36 COVID-19 claims on CORD-19 after training on the 1.4K-claim SciFact dataset.
methodology: Constructed a 1.4K expert-written claim dataset paired with evidence-containing abstracts, annotated with support/refute labels and rationale sentences; trained baseline models jointly with a Wikipedia claim dataset.
why_it_matters: This is the foundational benchmark the entire claim-verification literature (including CiteME, SciVer, CLAIM-BENCH) argues with or extends, so its label definitions and evidence-selection framing set the terms against which every later accuracy number must be read.
limitations: small dataset (1.4K claims), narrow biomedical/COVID domain test
predates LLM-era extraction pipelines, so no measurement of full-paper claim extraction accuracy
relevance_reason: Explicitly named in the brief as the SciFact line; the origin benchmark for scientific claim-evidence verification.

key_finding: Across 1,664 annotated samples from 180 papers, a substantial performance gap persists between the best of 11 benchmarked multimodal foundation models and human baselines, with figure-based verification remaining especially hard.
methodology: New cross-modal dataset built by modifying supporting figures/tables (rather than claims or LLM-fabricated contradictions) to create authentic refuted claims; tables provided in image, LaTeX, HTML and JSON formats; benchmarked 11 open and proprietary multimodal models.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a rigorous, artifact-resistant method for constructing refutation examples (perturbing evidence, not claims), directly informing what benchmark numbers can legitimately support and where figure-grounded evidence linking remains a hard, unsolved failure mode.
limitations: single evaluation snapshot across only ML/NLP/medicine domains
does not test abstention or calibrated uncertainty
relevance_reason: Directly answers the benchmark-construction question (C3) with a construction method designed to avoid inflating accuracy, and characterizes modality-specific evidence-linking failure.

key_finding: Raw LLM outputs for scientific reasoning graph extraction pass strict semantic validity gates 0/350 times on ARCHE; PEARL's repair layer raises this to 300/350 and improves average REA from 0.339 to 0.906.
methodology: Training-free repair framework applying a closed Peircean schema and evidence-grounded judge feedback to fix malformed edges, drifting labels, incorrect root orientation and weak source anchors in LLM-generated reasoning graphs, tested on five 70-paper archives from the ARCHE benchmark.
why_it_matters: A near-total baseline failure rate (0/350) on raw LLM graph extraction directly contradicts the premise that frontier LLMs extract claims/evidence structure reliably; the taxonomy of failure types (malformed syntax, wrong root, weak anchors) maps closely onto the evidence-link error categories the brief asks us to characterize.
limitations: single benchmark family (ARCHE), no cross-domain test outside its five archives
repair layer is post-hoc correction, not a measure of raw model calibration or abstention behaviour
relevance_reason: Provides concrete evidence that claim/evidence-graph extraction itself can fail almost completely before repair, directly challenging the brief's working premise.

key_finding: On identical agent outputs, measured unsupported-citation rate ranges from about 3% to 18% depending purely on verifier strictness, and verifiers disagree sharply on which citations to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27-0.30), so no single flag set is trustworthy without a named, calibrated protocol.
methodology: Gold-anchored evaluation protocol validating the verifier against human gold, a swappable verifier (recall 0.94 on supported class), BM25 re-attribution, and a split-conformal guard giving a distribution-free finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations; validated across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on SciFact, QASA and PubMedQA.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's abstention/calibration question with a deployable conformal guarantee and a concrete recalibration recipe for deployment drift, while showing that citation-faithfulness numbers are themselves unreliable unless the verifier and protocol are specified — this should change how the decision engine reports and bounds trustworthiness rather than just accepting a single verifier's verdict.
limitations: guarantee is on catch rate, not on whether the underlying conclusion is correct
tested on open 27-35B models; frontier closed models not covered
relevance_reason: Directly targets three of the five sub-criteria (evidence-link error characterization, benchmark legitimacy, and abstention/calibration) with quantified, cross-model, cross-pipeline results.

key_finding: Chart-derived evidence is encoded in VLM intermediate representations but fails to reach the prediction position, whereas this gap is absent for tables — a routing failure rather than an encoding failure, taking two architecturally distinct forms across model families.
methodology: Layer-wise linear probing and attention analysis on three open-weight VLMs comparing table vs. chart evidence representing identical underlying data.
why_it_matters: Explains a specific, previously unexplained mechanism behind one class of evidence-linking failure (modality-dependent grounding), suggesting the decision engine may need modality-aware routing checks rather than assuming uniform evidence-linking reliability across figure/table/text sources.
limitations: only three open-weight VLMs studied
narrow to table-vs-chart comparison, not general claim-evidence linking errors like fabrication or wrong-direction reads
relevance_reason: Provides mechanistic insight into why certain evidence types are harder to ground, relevant to characterizing evidence-link failure modes.

key_finding: Models that saturate existing claim-verification benchmarks consistently over-accept compositionally infeasible claims where a non-salient constraint is contradicted, revealing that existing benchmarks only test a shortcut 'salient-constraint checking' rather than genuine closed-world verification.
methodology: Constructed new compositionally infeasible claims (salient constraint supported, non-salient constraint contradicted) contrasted against standard single-perturbation infeasible claims; evaluated across model families and modalities, analyzed via ROC-curve positioning under context interventions.
why_it_matters: This is exactly the kind of benchmark-inflation finding the brief asks us to reach for: it shows current benchmarks cannot distinguish rigorous verification from a cheap shortcut, meaning reported high accuracy on standard claim-verification benchmarks overstates true reliability and should not be trusted as evidence that extraction/verification 'works well'.
limitations: focuses on constraint-level composition, not full extraction pipeline from raw papers
abstract does not report absolute accuracy numbers, only relative shortcut prevalence
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that current benchmarks validate robust verification, and shows an over-generalisation-like failure mode (accepting claims despite contradicted non-salient evidence).

key_finding: Across 3,000 expert-annotated multimodal claim-verification examples from 1,113 papers, a substantial performance gap remains between 21 state-of-the-art foundation models and human experts.
methodology: New benchmark with four reasoning-type subsets and expert-annotated supporting evidence per example; evaluated 21 multimodal models including o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Llama-3.2-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL, with RAG analysis and human error evaluation.
why_it_matters: A large, expert-annotated, fine-grained-evidence benchmark that quantifies exactly how far multimodal claim verification is from expert-level performance, giving a concrete numeric baseline the project's trustworthiness reporting should be measured against rather than assuming near-human competence.
limitations: benchmark evaluation only, no analysis of whether errors are extraction vs. linking vs. reasoning failures in fine detail
no abstention/calibration testing reported
relevance_reason: A major, well-constructed multimodal claim-evidence grounding benchmark directly answering the benchmark-construction sub-question.

key_finding: Equipping a VLM with type-aware visual tools (table focus, chart-to-structure parsing, region zoom) trained via GRPO outperforms prompting-based and RL-based tool-use baselines on SciVer and MuSciClaims across five VLMs from three model families.
methodology: Tool-augmented reinforcement learning framework with a composite reward (correctness, format, length, tool-use efficiency/validity) trained with GRPO; evaluated on Qwen, InternVL, and Gemma model families.
why_it_matters: Shows a concrete engineering path (explicit tool calls for structured visual evidence) that reduces one class of evidence-linking error, useful if the decision engine needs to ground claims in figures/tables rather than relying on end-to-end VLM reading.
limitations: evaluated only on two closely related benchmarks (SciVer, MuSciClaims)
no test of calibration/abstention or generalisation beyond scientific claim verification datasets
relevance_reason: A methods paper directly targeting the evidence-linking failure modes (locating and reading visual evidence) central to the brief's second question.

key_finding: Citation-based metrics (section coverage, citation accuracy) separate the eight evaluated models far more clearly than LLM-evaluator rubric scores, which remain tightly compressed across models; open-weight models approach closed-model citation accuracy at 3-6x lower latency.
methodology: 6,211 single-paper QA pairs from 494 open-access papers across eight domains and four question types (lookup, comprehension, multi-hop, adversarial), evaluated with a deterministic citation matcher plus an LLM rubric evaluator, explicitly rewarding grounded refusal when the source does not support an answer.
why_it_matters: Shows that citation-grounding metrics and LLM-judge scores diverge sharply — a direct caution for how the decision engine should measure trustworthiness, and its adversarial/refusal-reward design is exactly the abstention behaviour the brief asks whether it helps or just costs coverage.
limitations: abstract does not report the coverage cost of grounded refusal quantitatively
single-paper QA setting, not full multi-document claim extraction
relevance_reason: Directly relevant to benchmark construction and abstention/calibration questions with a citation-grounded, refusal-aware evaluation design.

key_finding: +VeriRel, which incorporates verification success into document ranking, consistently outperforms off-the-shelf IR ranking for evidence retrieval on SciFact, SciFact-Open and Check-Covid, with positive downstream impact on verification.
methodology: Modifies document retrieval ranking to incorporate verification-success feedback rather than pure relevance; evaluated on three existing scientific fact-checking datasets.
why_it_matters: A retrieval-stage improvement that could reduce fabricated or irrelevant evidence links upstream of claim verification, but it is a narrow IR method-improvement rather than a finding about extraction accuracy or benchmark validity.
limitations: evaluated only on existing SciFact-family benchmarks, no new construction critique
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes
does not address abstention or cross-model generalisation
relevance_reason: Marginally related via improving evidence retrieval for scientific fact-checking, but contributes little to the core extraction-accuracy or benchmark-validity questions.

key_finding: Across over 300 claim-evidence pairs and six LLMs, closed-source models (GPT-4, Claude) consistently outperform open-source models in precision and recall on claim-evidence extraction, and strategically designed multi-pass prompting significantly improves linking accuracy at higher computational cost.
methodology: CLAIM-BENCH benchmark comparing three divide-and-conquer-inspired extraction strategies (including three-pass and one-by-one prompting) across six diverse LLMs on full-length papers across multiple research domains.
why_it_matters: Directly measures claim-evidence extraction accuracy broken down by model and prompting strategy on full papers, giving concrete evidence for whether extraction accuracy (not just evidence linking) varies by model — a core input to question 1 of the brief.
limitations: abstract does not report accuracy broken down by paper section or claim type in detail
cost-accuracy tradeoff of multi-pass prompting may not scale to production pipelines
relevance_reason: A dedicated benchmark for claim-evidence extraction accuracy and linking across models, directly answering the brief's first two questions.

key_finding: On the CiteME benchmark, frontier LMs achieve only 4.2-18.5% accuracy at identifying the paper referenced by a text excerpt, versus 69.7% for humans; an autonomous search-and-read agent (CiteAgent, GPT-4o-based) raises this to 35.3%.
methodology: Benchmark of text excerpts from recent ML papers each referencing a single other paper, evaluated for citation-attribution accuracy across frontier LMs and a retrieval-augmented agent system.
why_it_matters: A stark, direct measurement showing citation-grounding is nowhere near reliable even for frontier models, which should recalibrate the project's confidence that evidence-linking failures are a minor residual problem rather than a dominant one.
limitations: citation attribution (finding the source paper) is a narrower task than full evidence-passage grounding within a paper
confined to machine learning papers
relevance_reason: Explicitly named in the brief's known papers; provides the headline evidence that citation grounding is unreliable even in frontier models.

key_finding: Top-tier LLMs achieve high sentence-attribution performance but with high hallucination rates; a metadata-augmented, RAG-based approach with Mistral reduces hallucination rates by 42% on indirect queries while maintaining competitive precision, though adversarial testing exposes fundamental limitations linking titles to abstracts.
methodology: REASONS dataset with sentence-level citation annotations across 12 arXiv domains, covering indirect (sentence-to-title) and direct (author attribution) query scenarios; tested GPT-o1, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, DeepSeek and smaller models like Perplexity AI (7B), with and without metadata/RAG augmentation.
why_it_matters: Quantifies hallucination as the key reliability metric for citation attribution rather than raw accuracy alone, and shows a concrete mitigation (RAG + metadata) with a measured 42% reduction — directly useful evidence for how the decision engine should measure and reduce fabricated-support errors.
limitations: adversarial testing reveals persistent title-to-abstract linking failures not solved by the proposed mitigation
no test of abstention/calibrated refusal as a trustworthiness mechanism
relevance_reason: Provides a cross-model, cross-domain benchmark quantifying hallucination in citation attribution and a mitigation strategy, relevant to evidence-link error characterization and benchmark construction.

key_finding: On the ALCE benchmark, even the best LLM-based systems fail to fully support their citations 50% of the time on the ELI5 dataset, revealing large gaps in citation quality despite fluent-looking output.
methodology: Introduces ALCE, an end-to-end benchmark requiring retrieval plus citation-annotated generation across diverse questions/corpora, with automatic metrics for fluency, correctness, and citation quality validated against human judgment.
why_it_matters: This is the precursor benchmark-construction methodology (automatic + human-correlated citation-quality metrics) that CiteME-style scientific grounding benchmarks build on, so it recalibrates what 'benchmark numbers can legitimately support' for citation grounding claims — but its setting is open-domain QA, not scientific-paper claim extraction, so its accuracy figures cannot be imported directly.
limitations: general open-domain QA (ELI5, etc.), not scientific literature
citations are to retrieved passages/web sources rather than paper-internal evidence or tables
predates the brief's 2024-01 window
relevance_reason: Foundational benchmark-construction work for LLM citation evaluation that the newer scientific claim-grounding benchmarks (e.g. CiteME) build on methodologically.

key_finding: Human audit of four commercial generative search engines found only 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by citations and only 74.5% of citations actually supported their associated statement.
methodology: Human evaluation of citation precision and recall across Bing Chat, NeevaAI, perplexity.ai, and YouChat, using a diverse query set from Google logs, Reddit, and other sources.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the base rate of unsupported and inaccurate citations in LLM-generated, citation-bearing text (roughly a quarter of citations wrong), which is the closest empirical analogue to the evidence-linking error rates the paper-to-decision engine must anticipate and calibrate abstention against — but it measures web-search citation behavior, not scientific-paper claim grounding, so the numbers should inform expectations rather than be treated as transferable accuracy figures.
limitations: domain is open-web generative search engines, not scientific papers
citations are to web sources, not paper text/tables/figures
predates the brief's 2024-01 window and the systems evaluated are proprietary black boxes
relevance_reason: Provides rigorous quantitative evidence of pervasive citation-support failures in LLM systems, directly informing the brief's C2 question on evidence-link error rates, despite being in a different domain (web search) than scientific-paper grounding.
